title: On Language Drift during RLVR Post-Training

paper.title: On Language Drift during RLVR Post-Training
paper.abstract: Abstract Recent advances in LLM reasoning models—driven primarily by the paradigm of post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR)—have enabled them to accomplish impressively complex tasks. However, in parallel with their rising capabilities, LLMs have increasingly displayed signs of language drift in their chains of thought (CoTs): unusual, non-standard, and seemingly nonsensical language use. Although it is well-documented—and can potentially impair CoT monitorability—the causes of language drift are thus far poorly understood. In this paper, we identify the conditions under which language drift occurs: we prove theoretically that RLVR optimization pressure permits unbounded language drift, while supervised fine-tuning does not. We then show empirically that language drift specifically arises during RLVR on novel reasoning tasks—i.e. when the target behavior cannot be drawn out of the base model. Finally, we prove that it is not possible to constrain language drift without constraining expected reward, suggesting that CoT monitorability cannot be improved without harming performance during RLVR post-training at the frontier.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent, drastic gains in the reasoning capabilities of frontier models have enabled LLM-based agents to solve increasingly complex, long-horizon coding tasks ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , solve long-standing mathematical problems ( Alon et al., 2026 , e.g.) , etc. These impressive and rapid improvements have been driven primarily by scaling reinforcement learning (RL; OpenAI, 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 , etc.) —in particular, reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), which optimizes for deterministic, outcome-based rewards such as final-answer correctness. Figure 1 : SFT (left) on prompt/CoT/answer triples ( x , z , y ) (x,z,y) does not permit a model π ( SFT ) \pi^{(\textit{SFT})} to drift arbitrarily far from a human language distribution P ( HL ) {P^{(\textit{HL})}} while minimizing cross-entropy with a target distribution D ( SFT ) {{D}^{(\textit{SFT})}} . RLVR (right) places no optimization pressure on the CoT z z , allowing arbitrary language drift away from natural language in the reasoning trace. The example completions in this figure were drawn from Llama-3.2-1B models trained via SFT and RLVR (respectively) on GSM8K. However, frontier LLMs have simultaneously been displaying increasing degrees of language drift: novel linguistic behavior that is non-standard and/or ungrammatical—and occasionally illegible—to human readers ( Lazaridou et al., 2020 ) . As an example, the RLVR-trained model in Figure 1 has undergone language drift, affecting not only the style of its reasoning trace, but also the interpretation of the reference (meaning) of the terms that it uses. In particular, it conflates the cost of the dog—which is not relevant or stated—with the cost of the grooming. Language drift is naturally frustrating to users, who struggle to parse the atypical constructions and idiosyncratic vocabulary use displayed by LLM agents. The ubiquity and severity of this problem are such that attempted workarounds have become frequent topics of online discussion: skills 1 1 1 e.g. https://github.com/danyuchn/asd-ste100-skill . instructing models to use only ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English, “Claudish-to-English translators” (see Figure 2 ), etc. Beyond user frustration with difficult prose, more extreme degrees of language drift (see e.g. Figure 3 ) pose a more serious threat in the form of decreased chain of thought (CoT) monitorability ( Baker et al., 2025 ; Korbak et al., 2025 ) : illegible CoTs—either to humans or other LLMs—render models’ internal reasoning processes more opaque, leading to difficulty in determining intent and predicting future actions. This consequence of language drift is particularly worrisome in light of safety concerns due to recent security incidents involving unintended LLM agent behavior 2 2 2 e.g. the OpenAI Hugging Face hacking incident . . Figure 2 : “Claudish”—language in the idiosyncratic style of Anthropic’s Claude models—translated to its plain-English equivalent. This example was taken from the ProgramAsWeights Claudish-to-English translator . Despite its prevalence and potential consequences, the reasons for language drift remain poorly understood. Although RLVR has been suggested as a potential culprit ( Korbak et al., 2025 ) , it has thus far been unclear whether language drift can occur purely due to RLVR optimization pressure. In this paper, we answer this question in the affirmative: namely, we prove theoretically that RLVR training alone permits unbounded language drift, while supervised fine-tuning (SFT) prevents language drift beyond a fixed, finite upper bound (see Figure 1 ; Section 4 ). We additionally prove in Section 4 that constraining language drift necessarily constrains reward , in the sense that limiting the degree of language drift that an LLM can undergo during RLVR training limits the maximum expected reward that the model can attain. This result supports arguments that maintaining CoT monitorability may not be possible without hindering downstream performance ( Baker et al., 2025 , e.g.) . We then investigate the precise cause of language drift. We argue that language drift is simply a special case of novel behavior—namely, novel linguistic behavior. Given that novel behavior arises during RLVR when behavior sharpening —drawing target reasoning behavior out of the base model—is not possible ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , we hypothesize that language drift occurs as a side-effect of novel behavior discovery during RLVR on novel tasks . In Section 5 , we provide empirical evidence in support of this hypothesis, demonstrating that when behavior sharpening is not possible, models display greater degrees of language drift during RLVR than during SFT. We further provide evidence that different RLVR training runs starting from the same model—and trained on the same dataset—develop distinct linguistic behavior: i.e. each RLVR training run undergoes unique language drift . A potential consequence of this finding is that even models trained on the same tasks may not be able to monitor the CoTs of an LLM that has undergone sufficient language drift. Figure 3 : Example of illegible internal reasoning uncovered during the METR evaluation of OpenAI’s GPT-5 . Taken together, these findings paint a troubling picture of the future balance between LLM safety and capability. Namely, language drift occurs during RLVR on novel reasoning tasks—precisely those tasks which must be conquered to advance the frontier—and cannot be constrained without harming expected performance. This conclusion raises the question: as frontier models advance to human-level capability and beyond, will it remain possible to monitor their reasoning traces in order to verify alignment?

sections.heading: Language Drift during RL.
sections.text: LLMs often exhibit nonsensical linguistic patterns under RLHF-style ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) optimization pressure: for example, models can learn to repeatedly generate the same token when using rewards derived from a neural sentiment-analysis classifier ( Korbak et al., 2022 ) . While this certainly qualifies as language drift in the narrowest sense, we exclude such reward-hacking-like phenomena from our analysis, and focus instead on the development of novel—but internally coherent—linguistic behavior. To that end, Mordatch and Abbeel (2018) study the emergence of communicative behavior resembling language during multi-agent RL with a limited action space and simple, RNN-based agents initialized from scratch. They find that goal-based reward provides sufficient optimization pressure for these agents to invent language-like, compositional communication codes over an abstract set of symbols. Similarly, Lazaridou et al. (2020) observe language drift—including shifting word meanings—when training LSTM-based ( Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997 ) language models to play referential games via multi-agent RL. These studies demonstrate that RL optimization pressure can cause linguistic invention in settings targeting communication ability. Our results in Section 5 extend these findings to more general and widely used reasoning settings, and to modern transformer architectures and RLVR algorithms.

sections.heading: Illegible Reasoning Traces.
sections.text: Guo et al. (2025) report that DeepSeek-R1-Zero exhibits ‘‘poor readability and language mixing’’ 3 3 3 It is unclear to what degree language mixing represents genuine language drift in the sense of Definition 1 , as language mixing is also well-documented in bilingual human language users ( Poplack, 1980 , in the form of code-switching; see e.g.) . , in particular switching between English and Chinese. Although adding a language-specific penalty improves readability, it harms performance: this finding is consistent with our theoretical result in Section 4.2 (Theorem 3 ) that language drift cannot be constrained without negatively impacting expected reward. Jose (2025) finds that frontier reasoning models sometimes output illegible and (seemingly) nonsensical CoTs within otherwise valid reasoning traces. Furthermore, removing these illegible portions of the reasoning traces considerably harms performance, suggesting that although the text may be nonsensical to human readers, it is still useful for—and therefore legible to—the LLM. Panfilov et al. (2026) similarly find human-illegible text in frontier models’ internal reasoning traces. Our theoretical and empirical findings in Sections 4 - 5 shed light on these results demonstrating language drift in SoTA, RLVR-trained reasoning models. In particular, our results suggest that this observed language drift arose during RLVR post-training on novel reasoning tasks.

sections.heading: Inducing Novel Linguistic Behavior.
sections.text: Vaduguru et al. (2026) use DPO-style preference optimization ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) to train LLMs to perform ad-hoc linguistic convention formation in multi-turn dialog settings. Although these authors deliberately pressure LLMs to develop unique linguistic behavior, their objective is efficiency in agent-human communication, and their training method therefore cannot induce (nor does it target) arbitrary language drift. Zhu et al. (2026) use prompting-based methods to compress text into human-illegible form—without substantially impacting its LLM-legibility—in order to condense models’ context windows without information loss. While this method merely elicits language drift potential already present in the model (as it relies purely on prompting), it demonstrates that LLMs do not necessarily need to operate over human-legible language.

sections.heading: 3 Preliminaries
sections.text: We focus our analysis in this work on text-based reasoning LLMs: models that produce a CoT and an answer, given a prompt. We deliberately exclude multimodal models for the sake of analytical tractability, and leave an investigation of such models to future work. As such, we treat an LLM as a conditional probability distribution π {\pi} over 𝒵 × 𝒴 \mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Y} given 𝒳 \mathcal{X} —i.e. over pairs ( z , y ) (z,y) of CoTs z z and answers y y , given a prompt x x .

sections.heading: 4.3 Hypothesis: Novel Tasks Induce Language Drift
sections.text: Theorem 1 implies that RLVR permits a given training run to undergo an arbitrary degree of language drift, while continuing to maximize expected reward. Theorem 3 goes further, and states that language drift must occur to maximize expected reward. These theorems do not, however, establish the degree of language drift that must occur during practical RLVR training: for some task/model pairs, it is likely the case that only a minimal amount of language drift is required to achieve a practically acceptable expected reward. In other words, we do not establish the (likely task-dependent) steepness of the curve in Figure 5 . As such, it is entirely possible that some SFT run undergoes a higher degree of language drift than an RLVR training run on the same task. The point is rather that the maximum possible language drift that an RLVR training run can undergo is unbounded, and therefore greater than the maximum of an SFT run. This is to say that while RLVR provides a setting in which language drift can arise, it does not in itself cause language drift to occur. In fact, RL’s Razor ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) posits that RL prefers to find solutions with minimal KL divergence to the base model, which seemingly suggests that RLVR tends to not lead to language drift. This aligns with recent findings that RLVR simply sharpens distributions, i.e. only draws out reasoning patterns already present in the base model ( Yue et al., 2025 ) . However, Liu et al. (2025) find that LLMs can in fact develop novel behavior under RLVR, when training on novel reasoning tasks. We argue that—absent optimization pressure on the CoT z z —those same pressures driving novel behavior development similarly increase the likelihood that novel linguistic behavior (i.e. language drift) arises: we hypothesize that language drift occurs as a side-effect of novel behavior discovery during RLVR over novel reasoning tasks . Conversely, we argue that language drift does not occur when the targeted reasoning task is not novel to the model: by definition, a non-novel task can be solved by drawing behavior out of the base model (behavior sharpening). In this case, RL’s Razor implies that the lowest-KL path—behavior sharpening—will be preferred, and therefore no meaningful language drift will occur.

sections.text: We first aim to demonstrate empirically our theoretical findings in Section 4.1 that RLVR permits greater language drift than SFT. Our second objective is to validate our hypothesis laid out in Section 4.3 that novel tasks in particular induce language drift in the context of RLVR training. sections.heading: 5.1 Methodology
sections.text: To evaluate the difference in language drift between SFT and RLVR, we trained the base models using both training methods. We employed the DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) variant of GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) as our RLVR implementation.

sections.heading: 5.1.1 Training and Validation
sections.text: For all three models, we first performed RLVR and SFT hyperparameter grid searches to identify the best-performing configuration for each training method (further details are located in Appendix B.1 ). We then replicated the optimal-hyperparameter run for each model and training method across five random seeds, for a total of 30 training runs. During training and validation, the models were prompted with two fixed few-shot examples (see Figure 8 in the Appendix). During validation and RLVR training, we limited the models to 256 generated tokens. Answers were submitted using the format “####{ANSWER}”, and we extracted the final answer detected in the model’s response to compute reward/correctness.

sections.heading: Iso-Performance Checkpoint Selection.
sections.text: For each training run, we selected for evaluation the highest-scoring checkpoint on a validation set of 128 withheld examples. However, the Llama and Gemma SFT runs consistently outperformed their RLVR counterparts. To control for any possible confounding relationship between final validation performance and language drift, we additionally selected the checkpoint from each SFT run with the closest validation score to that of the RLVR run for the same model and seed: we refer to these checkpoints as iso-SFT during evaluation. On the other hand, the Qwen RLVR checkpoints consistently outperformed SFT: we therefore also selected the checkpoint from each Qwen RLVR run with the closest validation score to that of the Qwen SFT run with the same seed ( iso-RLVR ).

sections.heading: Behavior-Sharpening Detection.
sections.text: As discussed above, we extracted the final submitted answer for validation and RLVR training reward. However, as base models, all three untrained LLMs failed to stop after emitting an answer to the prompted question; instead, they simply continued generating in-distribution question/trace/answer triples until the length limit was reached. As such, we computed accuracy for the base LLMs relative to both the first and last submitted answer, in order to obtain a rough estimate of the models’ propensity for behavior sharpening: if an LLM has a high first-submitted answer accuracy and a low last-submitted answer accuracy, then to achieve a high reward, it needs only learn to emit the EOS token after submitting the answer (rather than generate another question). In this case, the model clearly does not need to discover new behavior, and so RLVR can solve the task primarily through behavior sharpening.

sections.heading: 5.1.2 Evaluation
sections.text: As discussed in Section 3 , we do not have access to the human language distribution P ( HL ) {P^{(\textit{HL})}} . As such, it is not possible to directly measure language drift in these experiments. We instead use three instruct models to approximate P ( HL ) {P^{(\textit{HL})}} : Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct 8 8 8 https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct , Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct 9 9 9 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct , and OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct 10 10 10 https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct ( Walsh et al., 2024 ) . Although by our own arguments made throughout this paper, all three of those post-trained LLMs have themselves undergone an unknown degree of language drift from P ( HL ) {P^{(\textit{HL})}} , it is exceedingly unlikely that three distinct models have drifted to the same point in probability space. As such, we argue that by averaging over the three models, we can obtain a noisy triangulation of P ( HL ) {P^{(\textit{HL})}} . Even with this instruct-model-derived approximation of P ( HL ) {P^{(\textit{HL})}} , computing the full KL divergence between two LLMs is still intractable. We therefore measure relative language drift using CoT legibility as a proxy: the more an external reader is able to follow the CoT of an LLM, the less language drift that LLM has undergone.

sections.heading: Trace Legibility.
sections.text: We implement an experimental design based on those used in Wang et al. (2025) and Roytburg et al. (2026) . First, for each checkpoint π {\pi} selected after training in Section 5.1 (i.e. best-performing and iso-SFT/RLVR) and each prompt x x in the GSM8K validation set, we sample a reasoning trace and answer ( z , y ) ∼ π ⁡ ( – | x ) (z,y)\sim{\pi}(\text{\textendash}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx) . For each partial trace, each of the three instruct models is prompted to guess the final answer y y , based on the reasoning produced by π {\pi} up to that point. By measuring the degree to which the instruct models are able to follow z z , this experiment provides an estimate of the legibility of the CoT—and therefore an estimate of the (lack of) language drift undergone by π {\pi} . sections.heading: Self-Legibility.
sections.text: We perform an additional round of trace legibility experiments, in which we replace the instruct-model CoT readers with other models of the same type and trained with the same method (SFT/RLVR) as π \pi . For example, if the target model π \pi is a Gemma model trained with RLVR, we replace the instruct models with the other four Gemma RLVR runs (i.e. the other four seeds). We refer to this experiment as self-legibility . The goal of the self-legibility experiment is to measure the regularity (conversely, novelty) of language drift. If, for example, traces generated by an RLVR-trained model are more legible to other RLVR-trained models, we may conclude that RLVR-trained models tend to drift linguistically in the same direction in probability space. Conversely, if traces generated by an RLVR-trained model are less legible to other RLVR-trained models, then we may conclude that the direction of RLVR-induced language drift is unpredictable. Additional details regarding the configuration of the trace legibility and self-legibility experiments are located in Appendix B.2 .

sections.heading: CoT Utility Sanity Check.
sections.text: For each training run, we confirm that the model is in fact utilizing its generated reasoning traces to produce final answers, rather than producing performative CoTs ( Boppana et al., 2026 ) , invisible reasoning ( Baherwani et al., 2026 ) , etc. A discussion of our methodology and results is located in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Novel Tasks Induce Language Drift.
sections.text: In Figure 7 , we plot for each model the difference between mean RLVR legibility and mean SFT legibility: values less than zero indicate that the SFT traces were more legible than the RLVR traces at that fraction. We expect the differences at earlier fractions to be near zero, as a final answer is extremely difficult to guess when given less than half of the corresponding trace, regardless of whether it was generated by RLVR- or SFT-trained models. The plots in Figure 7 are summarized by the area-under-the-curve (AUC) values in Table 2 . Llama and Gemma have negative values for trace legibility and self-legibility, both when comparing best-performing checkpoints and when comparing the training methods at iso-performance. This indicates that both models have higher degrees of language drift 11 11 11 We record anecdotal, qualitative examples of novel linguistic behavior from Llama and Gemma in Appendix D . across the board under RLVR, which is consistent with Theorems 1 - 2 . That the Llama traces display higher degrees of language drift than Gemma is to be expected, as Gemma achieves much lower accuracy than Llama: when a task is too difficult, GRPO-style RL algorithms have very sparse gradients, and the LLM’s weights therefore cannot drift very far from those of the base model. As predicted by the hypothesis in Section 4.3 , Qwen—the only model that performs behavior sharpening during RLVR—is the only model for which RLVR exhibits virtually no language drift relative to SFT.

sections.heading: RLVR-Induced Language Drift is Unique.
sections.text: The results of the self-legibility experiment indicate that the RLVR-trained Llama and Gemma models have a lower degree of mutual legibility than their SFT-trained counterparts. This indicates that each RLVR-trained run drifted in a different direction, which in turn indicates that each run developed unique linguistic behavior. Conversely, Qwen—the only model that did not undergo RLVR-induced language drift as measured by trace legibility—is the only model type for which the RLVR-trained models have a higher degree of mutual legibility than the SFT-trained models.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we presented evidence that RLVR on novel tasks induces language drift in LLMs. In Section 4 , we proved theoretically that there is a finite upper bound on the maximum possible language drift that can occur during SFT, while no such upper bound exists for RLVR. Furthermore, we proved that language drift cannot be constrained during RLVR training without constraining expected reward (Theorem 3 ). We then demonstrated empirically that LLMs undergo a greater degree of language drift under RLVR than under SFT, when behavior sharpening is not viable—i.e. when the task is novel to the base model (Section 5 ). We furthermore showed that such RLVR-induced drift is unique, in that models of the same type trained on different seeds suffer from decreased mutual legibility. The implications of these findings with respect to frontier-model CoT monitorability are considerable. In particular, the conditions under which RLVR induces language drift—novel reasoning tasks—are precisely those under which models must be trained in order to advance the frontier. Furthermore, these are precisely the conditions under which RLVR is most needed, due to the difficulty of obtaining sufficient amounts of SFT data on novel reasoning environments. It then follows from Theorem 3 that we must accept increasing degrees of language drift in order to continue advancing the frontier with RLVR. Finally, that RLVR-induced language drift is unique—even among models initialized from the same base and trained on the same task—indicates that it is unpredictable: a given model can drift linguistically in multiple possible directions during RLVR training. This suggests that even a model trained on the same data as some target model π {\pi} cannot necessarily be relied upon to effectively comprehend—and therefore, monitor—the internal reasoning traces produced by π {\pi} .

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Due to resource constraints, we used only small, 1-1.5B models in our experiments. The use of such models naturally limits the size and difficulty of the reasoning datasets that they can be trained on: while we undeniably observe language drift in the Llama and Gemma models (see Appendix D ), this drift does not reach the degree of illegibility displayed in some frontier-model internal reasoning traces (e.g. in Figure 3 ). Due to the restricted range of datasets that these small models can be trained on, we were only able to find one dataset (GSM8K) that both contained annotated CoTs and that could be learned through RLVR and SFT by the three base models (Llama, Gemma, and Qwen; see Section 5.1 ). In future versions of this manuscript, we intend to extend the results of our experiments in Section 5 with additional reasoning datasets. Finally, our experiments in Section 5 primarily pertain to Theorems 1 - 2 and our hypothesis in Section 4.3 : we do not include any empirical demonstration of our theoretical findings in Section 4.2 (Theorem 3 ) that constraining language drift necessarily constrains expected reward. We likewise intend to update future versions of the manuscript with experiments to this end.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.02015v1 [cs.LG] 01 Oct 2026 On Language Drift during RLVR Post-Training Michael Sullivan Affiliation: Department of Language Science and Technology, Saarland University, Saarbrücken, Germany Correspondence to: msullivan@lst.uni-saarland.de Alexander Koller Affiliation: Department of Language Science and Technology, Saarland University, Saarbrücken, Germany Abstract Recent advances in LLM reasoning models—driven primarily by the paradigm of post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR)—have enabled them to accomplish impressively complex tasks. However, in parallel with their rising capabilities, LLMs have increasingly displayed signs of language drift in their chains of thought (CoTs): unusual, non-standard, and seemingly nonsensical language use. Although it is well-documented—and can potentially impair CoT monitorability—the causes of language drift are thus far poorly understood. In this paper, we identify the conditions under which language drift occurs: we prove theoretically that RLVR optimization pressure permits unbounded language drift, while supervised fine-tuning does not. We then show empirically that language drift specifically arises during RLVR on novel reasoning tasks—i.e. when the target behavior cannot be drawn out of the base model. Finally, we prove that it is not possible to constrain language drift without constraining expected reward, suggesting that CoT monitorability cannot be improved without harming performance during RLVR post-training at the frontier. Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML 1 Introduction Recent, drastic gains in the reasoning capabilities of frontier models have enabled LLM-based agents to solve increasingly complex, long-horizon coding tasks ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , solve long-standing mathematical problems ( Alon et al., 2026 , e.g.) , etc. These impressive and rapid improvements have been driven primarily by scaling reinforcement learning (RL; OpenAI, 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 , etc.) —in particular, reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), which optimizes for deterministic, outcome-based rewards such as final-answer correctness. Figure 1 : SFT (left) on prompt/CoT/answer triples ( x , z , y ) (x,z,y) does not permit a model π ( SFT ) \pi^{(\textit{SFT})} to drift arbitrarily far from a human language distribution P ( HL ) {P^{(\textit{HL})}} while minimizing cross-entropy with a target distribution D ( SFT ) {{D}^{(\textit{SFT})}} . RLVR (right) places no optimization pressure on the CoT z z , allowing arbitrary language drift away from natural language in the reasoning trace. The example completions in this figure were drawn from Llama-3.2-1B models trained via SFT and RLVR (respectively) on GSM8K. However, frontier LLMs have simultaneously been displaying increasing degrees of language drift: novel linguistic behavior that is non-standard and/or ungrammatical—and occasionally illegible—to human readers ( Lazaridou et al., 2020 ) . As an example, the RLVR-trained model in Figure 1 has undergone language drift, affecting not only the style of its reasoning trace, but also the interpretation of the reference (meaning) of the terms that it uses. In particular, it conflates the cost of the dog—which is not relevant or stated—with the cost of the grooming. Language drift is naturally frustrating to users, who struggle to parse the atypical constructions and idiosyncratic vocabulary use displayed by LLM agents. The ubiquity and severity of this problem are such that attempted workarounds have become frequent topics of online discussion: skills 1 1 1 e.g. https://github.com/danyuchn/asd-ste100-skill . instructing models to use only ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English, “Claudish-to-English translators” (see Figure 2 ), etc. Beyond user frustration with difficult prose, more extreme degrees of language drift (see e.g. Figure 3 ) pose a more serious threat in the form of decreased chain of thought (CoT) monitorability ( Baker et al., 2025 ; Korbak et al., 2025 ) : illegible CoTs—either to humans or other LLMs—render models’ internal reasoning processes more opaque, leading to difficulty in determining intent and predicting future actions. This consequence of language drift is particularly worrisome in light of safety concerns due to recent security incidents involving unintended LLM agent behavior 2 2 2 e.g. the OpenAI Hugging Face hacking incident . . Figure 2 : “Claudish”—language in the idiosyncratic style of Anthropic’s Claude models—translated to its plain-English equivalent. This example was taken from the ProgramAsWeights Claudish-to-English translator . Despite its prevalence and potential consequences, the reasons for language drift remain poorly understood. Although RLVR has been suggested as a potential culprit ( Korbak et al., 2025 ) , it has thus far been unclear whether language drift can occur purely due to RLVR optimization pressure. In this paper, we answer this question in the affirmative: namely, we prove theoretically that RLVR training alone permits unbounded language drift, while supervised fine-tuning (SFT) prevents language drift beyond a fixed, finite upper bound (see Figure 1 ; Section 4 ). We additionally prove in Section 4 that constraining language drift necessarily constrains reward , in the sense that limiting the degree of language drift that an LLM can undergo during RLVR training limits the maximum expected reward that the model can attain. This result supports arguments that maintaining CoT monitorability may not be possible without hindering downstream performance ( Baker et al., 2025 , e.g.) . We then investigate the precise cause of language drift. We argue that language drift is simply a special case of novel behavior—namely, novel linguistic behavior. Given that novel behavior arises during RLVR when behavior sharpening —drawing target reasoning behavior out of the base model—is not possible ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , we hypothesize that language drift occurs as a side-effect of novel behavior discovery during RLVR on novel tasks . In Section 5 , we provide empirical evidence in support of this hypothesis, demonstrating that when behavior sharpening is not possible, models display greater degrees of language drift during RLVR than during SFT. We further provide evidence that different RLVR training runs starting from the same model—and trained on the same dataset—develop distinct linguistic behavior: i.e. each RLVR training run undergoes unique language drift . A potential consequence of this finding is that even models trained on the same tasks may not be able to monitor the CoTs of an LLM that has undergone sufficient language drift. Figure 3 : Example of illegible internal reasoning uncovered during the METR evaluation of OpenAI’s GPT-5 . Taken together, these findings paint a troubling picture of the future balance between LLM safety and capability. Namely, language drift occurs during RLVR on novel reasoning tasks—precisely those tasks which must be conquered to advance the frontier—and cannot be constrained without harming expected performance. This conclusion raises the question: as frontier models advance to human-level capability and beyond, will it remain possible to monitor their reasoning traces in order to verify alignment? 2 Related Work Language Drift during RL. LLMs often exhibit nonsensical linguistic patterns under RLHF-style ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) optimization pressure: for example, models can learn to repeatedly generate the same token when using rewards derived from a neural sentiment-analysis classifier ( Korbak et al., 2022 ) . While this certainly qualifies as language drift in the narrowest sense, we exclude such reward-hacking-like phenomena from our analysis, and focus instead on the development of novel—but internally coherent—linguistic behavior. To that end, Mordatch and Abbeel (2018) study the emergence of communicative behavior resembling language during multi-agent RL with a limited action space and simple, RNN-based agents initialized from scratch. They find that goal-based reward provides sufficient optimization pressure for these agents to invent language-like, compositional communication codes over an abstract set of symbols. Similarly, Lazaridou et al. (2020) observe language drift—including shifting word meanings—when training LSTM-based ( Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997 ) language models to play referential games via multi-agent RL. These studies demonstrate that RL optimization pressure can cause linguistic invention in settings targeting communication ability. Our results in Section 5 extend these findings to more general and widely used reasoning settings, and to modern transformer architectures and RLVR algorithms. Illegible Reasoning Traces. Guo et al. (2025) report that DeepSeek-R1-Zero exhibits ‘‘poor readability and language mixing’’ 3 3 3 It is unclear to what degree language mixing represents genuine language drift in the sense of Definition 1 , as language mixing is also well-documented in bilingual human language users ( Poplack, 1980 , in the form of code-switching; see e.g.) . , in particular switching between English and Chinese. Although adding a language-specific penalty improves readability, it harms performance: this finding is consistent with our theoretical result in Section 4.2 (Theorem 3 ) that language drift cannot be constrained without negatively impacting expected reward. Theorem 3 goes further, and states that language drift must occur to maximize expected reward. These theorems do not, however, establish the degree of language drift that must occur during practical RLVR training: for some task/model pairs, it is likely the case that only a minimal amount of language drift is required to achieve a practically acceptable expected reward. In other words, we do not establish the (likely task-dependent) steepness of the curve in Figure 5 . As such, it is entirely possible that some SFT run undergoes a higher degree of language drift than an RLVR training run on the same task. The point is rather that the maximum possible language drift that an RLVR training run can undergo is unbounded, and therefore greater than the maximum of an SFT run. This is to say that while RLVR provides a setting in which language drift can arise, it does not in itself cause language drift to occur. In fact, RL’s Razor ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) posits that RL prefers to find solutions with minimal KL divergence to the base model, which seemingly suggests that RLVR tends to not lead to language drift. This aligns with recent findings that RLVR simply sharpens distributions, i.e. only draws out reasoning patterns already present in the base model ( Yue et al., 2025 ) . However, Liu et al. (2025) find that LLMs can in fact develop novel behavior under RLVR, when training on novel reasoning tasks. We argue that—absent optimization pressure on the CoT z z —those same pressures driving novel behavior development similarly increase the likelihood that novel linguistic behavior (i.e. language drift) arises: we hypothesize that language drift occurs as a side-effect of novel behavior discovery during RLVR over novel reasoning tasks . Conversely, we argue that language drift does not occur when the targeted reasoning task is not novel to the model: by definition, a non-novel task can be solved by drawing behavior out of the base model (behavior sharpening). In this case, RL’s Razor implies that the lowest-KL path—behavior sharpening—will be preferred, and therefore no meaningful language drift will occur. 5 Experiments We first aim to demonstrate empirically our theoretical findings in Section 4.1 that RLVR permits greater language drift than SFT. Our second objective is to validate our hypothesis laid out in Section 4.3 that novel tasks in particular induce language drift in the context of RLVR training. We then replicated the optimal-hyperparameter run for each model and training method across five random seeds, for a total of 30 training runs. During training and validation, the models were prompted with two fixed few-shot examples (see Figure 8 in the Appendix). During validation and RLVR training, we limited the models to 256 generated tokens. Answers were submitted using the format “####{ANSWER}”, and we extracted the final answer detected in the model’s response to compute reward/correctness. Iso-Performance Checkpoint Selection. For each training run, we selected for evaluation the highest-scoring checkpoint on a validation set of 128 withheld examples. However, the Llama and Gemma SFT runs consistently outperformed their RLVR counterparts. To control for any possible confounding relationship between final validation performance and language drift, we additionally selected the checkpoint from each SFT run with the closest validation score to that of the RLVR run for the same model and seed: we refer to these checkpoints as iso-SFT during evaluation. On the other hand, the Qwen RLVR checkpoints consistently outperformed SFT: we therefore also selected the checkpoint from each Qwen RLVR run with the closest validation score to that of the Qwen SFT run with the same seed ( iso-RLVR ). Behavior-Sharpening Detection. As discussed above, we extracted the final submitted answer for validation and RLVR training reward. However, as base models, all three untrained LLMs failed to stop after emitting an answer to the prompted question; instead, they simply continued generating in-distribution question/trace/answer triples until the length limit was reached. As such, we computed accuracy for the base LLMs relative to both the first and last submitted answer, in order to obtain a rough estimate of the models’ propensity for behavior sharpening: if an LLM has a high first-submitted answer accuracy and a low last-submitted answer accuracy, then to achieve a high reward, it needs only learn to emit the EOS token after submitting the answer (rather than generate another question). In this case, the model clearly does not need to discover new behavior, and so RLVR can solve the task primarily through behavior sharpening. 5.1.2 Evaluation As discussed in Section 3 , we do not have access to the human language distribution P ( HL ) {P^{(\textit{HL})}} . The results of the self-legibility experiment indicate that the RLVR-trained Llama and Gemma models have a lower degree of mutual legibility than their SFT-trained counterparts. Conversely, Qwen—the only model that did not undergo RLVR-induced language drift as measured by trace legibility—is the only model type for which the RLVR-trained models have a higher degree of mutual legibility than the SFT-trained models. 6 Discussion and Conclusion In this paper, we presented evidence that RLVR on novel tasks induces language drift in LLMs. In Section 4 , we proved theoretically that there is a finite upper bound on the maximum possible language drift that can occur during SFT, while no such upper bound exists for RLVR. Furthermore, we proved that language drift cannot be constrained during RLVR training without constraining expected reward (Theorem 3 ). We then demonstrated empirically that LLMs undergo a greater degree of language drift under RLVR than under SFT, when behavior sharpening is not viable—i.e. when the task is novel to the base model (Section 5 ). We furthermore showed that such RLVR-induced drift is unique, in that models of the same type trained on different seeds suffer from decreased mutual legibility. The implications of these findings with respect to frontier-model CoT monitorability are considerable. In particular, the conditions under which RLVR induces language drift—novel reasoning tasks—are precisely those under which models must be trained in order to advance the frontier. Furthermore, these are precisely the conditions under which RLVR is most needed, due to the difficulty of obtaining sufficient amounts of SFT data on novel reasoning environments. It then follows from Theorem 3 that we must accept increasing degrees of language drift in order to continue advancing the frontier with RLVR. Finally, that RLVR-induced language drift is unique—even among models initialized from the same base and trained on the same task—indicates that it is unpredictable: a given model can drift linguistically in multiple possible directions during RLVR training. This suggests that even a model trained on the same data as some target model π {\pi} cannot necessarily be relied upon to effectively comprehend—and therefore, monitor—the internal reasoning traces produced by π {\pi} . Limitations Due to resource constraints, we used only small, 1-1.5B models in our experiments. The use of such models naturally limits the size and difficulty of the reasoning datasets that they can be trained on: while we undeniably observe language drift in the Llama and Gemma models (see Appendix D ), this drift does not reach the degree of illegibility displayed in some frontier-model internal reasoning traces (e.g. in Figure 3 ). Due to the restricted range of datasets that these small models can be trained on, we were only able to find one dataset (GSM8K) that both contained annotated CoTs and that could be learned through RLVR and SFT by the three base models (Llama, Gemma, and Qwen; see Section 5.1 ). In future versions of this manuscript, we intend to extend the results of our experiments in Section 5 with additional reasoning datasets. Finally, our experiments in Section 5 primarily pertain to Theorems 1 - 2 and our hypothesis in Section 4.3 : we do not include any empirical demonstration of our theoretical findings in Section 4.2 (Theorem 3 ) that constraining language drift necessarily constrains expected reward.
